items.title: Eddie Palmieri — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: my friend Manny Lopez was traveling with the Irakere, and he brought them to the studio when I was recording for CBS. They heard...Chucho Valdés heard Lucumi Macumba Voodoo.

ctx.x: So you’re diversified, but the root is from Africa.

Well, the idea was that it all related to the belief, the religious belief. Chango is Shango in Brazil. But the idea is that they were all captives that were brought in, and what happened to the development... I brought in the great percussionist, Francisco Aguabella. He sang there, he played the batas; it was quite accepted... As a matter of fact, my friend Manny Lopez was traveling with the Irakere, and he brought them to the studio when I was recording for CBS. They heard...Chucho Valdés heard Lucumi Macumba…
I want to go back a little bit and talk about some of the records that personally really galvanized me. Sentido, The Sun of Latin Music, of course... To me this is another landmark.
